front: TC030: What is the minimum viable move?
back: Before your next important conversation or presentation, notice your default physical behaviour. Set a still baseline. Move only when you mean to.

front: TC030: What is the core sequence?
back: Still baseline -> Deliberate movement -> Gestures that reinforce the point.

front: TC030: What is the field tip?
TC030: What is the strong version of: Constant fidgeting, rocking, or pacing while speaking?
back: Relaxed stillness as the default. Deliberate movement to punctuate key points.

front: TC030: What is the strong version of: Large gestures that do not match the verbal content?
back: Gestures that precisely reinforce what is being said. No more.

front: TC030: What is the strong version of: Shrinking posture — hunched, small, tight?
back: Natural upright alignment with relaxed shoulders. No performance, no contraction.

front: TC030: What is better than: (Shoulders up, joints locked, barely breathing)?
back: Still means settled — feet planted, shoulders down, breath moving.

front: TC030: What is better than: (Laps of the stage with no relationship to the content)?
back: Move to mark a new section, plant, and stay until the next one.

front: TC030: What is better than: (Hands illustrating every syllable)?
back: Rest the hands by default so the one gesture that matters still has somewhere to go.

front: TC030: What are signs it is working?
back: Your physical presence matches the gravity of what you are saying. Nervousness is not leaking into visible movement. People focus on your words rather than your body. You feel more grounded in your body during difficult conversations.

front: TC030: When should you avoid this technique?
back: In casual, high-energy social settings where measured movement reads as stiff or unnatural. When genuine urgency requires rapid physical movement.

front: TC030: What is the best recovery line?
back: 'I will put the pen down; it was doing my nerves out loud.'
